questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A nurse tells the truth to a patient even though the result may upset him, because truth-telling is her duty. Which theory guides her?
questions.rationale: Deontology holds that acts are right from duty and moral rules, independent of their consequences.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Deontological theories (PDF p. 33)
questions.quote: motives and actions are morally right' independent of their consequences

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: Kant's categorical imperative says to treat persons:
options: As ends, never only as means
questions.rationale: One formulation: treat yourself and others as ends in themselves and never only as a means to an end.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Categorical imperative (PDF p. 34)
questions.quote: treat both yourself and other people as ends in themselves and never only as a means to an end

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: In Kant's ethics, if a perfect duty conflicts with an imperfect duty:
questions.rationale: Perfect duties (e.g., truth-telling) bind without exception and prevail over imperfect duties (e.g., helping others).
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Perfect and imperfect duties (PDF p. 34)
questions.quote: In n conflict between a perfect and imperfect duty, perfect duty prevnils.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: During a disaster, the nurse gives scarce vaccines to benefit the most people. This reflects:
questions.rationale: Utilitarianism judges an act good if it brings the greatest happiness to the greatest number.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Teleological theories (PDF p. 35)
questions.quote: an action is good if it results in maximum satisfaction for a large number of people

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Which theory judges an act right if it serves the person's own self-interest?
questions.rationale: Ethical egoism holds an act is good if it maximizes the person's own self-interest, even at others' expense.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Teleological theories (PDF p. 35)
questions.quote: results that ma.ximize the person's self-interest

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: The view that right and wrong depend on each society's guidelines is:
questions.rationale: Cultural relativism says right and wrong depend on a society's moral guidelines, which vary by place and time.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Other ethical theories (PDF p. 36)
questions.quote: "Right- and "wrong" depend on a society's moral guidelines.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: Virtue ethics judges moral conduct mainly by the nurse's:
questions.rationale: Virtue ethics looks to personal traits (virtues) that dispose a person to choose rightly, not codes or outcomes.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Virtue ethics (PDF p. 36)
questions.quote: Ethical value is determined by character

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Plato's four classical virtues are justice, temperance, courage and:
questions.rationale: Plato's four classical virtues: justice, temperance, courage and wisdom.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Secular virtues (PDF p. 37)
questions.quote: justice, temperance, courage, and wisdom

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A nurse who fails to act with prudence is most at risk for:
questions.rationale: Prudence (phronesis) is careful analysis of actions; lack of prudence can lead to negligence or malpractice.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Practical wisdom (PDF p. 38)
questions.quote: Inability to bc prudent could lead to situations involving negligence or malpractice.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: The virtue that supports a nurse's accountability by keeping commitments is:
questions.rationale: Fidelity is faithfulness to agreements and commitments; it underpins accountability.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Virtues of the health care provider (PDF p. 38)
questions.quote: It is the main principle that supports the concept of accountability of nurses

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A competent patient refuses a blood transfusion after full explanation. The nurse respects the principle of:
questions.rationale: Autonomy is self-determination, including the right to accept or refuse treatment.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Autonomy (PDF p. 39)
questions.quote: It is the right to accept or refuse any treatment.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: A competent patient refuses a procedure. What should the nurse do first?
questions.rationale: Refusal is the patient's legal right: assess the reason, inform the physician and document it.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Consent (PDF p. 43)
questions.quote: First, you have to assess the reason for refusal

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which is one of the four requirements of informed consent?
questions.rationale: Requirements: decision-making capacity, documentation, disclosure and comprehension of information.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Informed consent (PDF p. 43)
questions.quote: I. decision- making capacity

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: The nurse finds the surgical patient received morphine 30 minutes ago and consent is not yet signed. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Consent must be obtained when the patient is not under opioids; the person doing the procedure obtains it.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Informed consent (PDF p. 44)
questions.quote: when the patient is not under the influence of medication such as opioids/narcotic analgesics

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Who is responsible for obtaining informed consent for surgery?
questions.rationale: The person performing the procedure obtains informed consent; the nurse may witness the signature.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Informed consent (PDF p. 44)
questions.quote: The person responsible (or performing the procedure is responsible for obtaining the informed consent

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Which condition justifies emergency treatment without consent?
questions.rationale: Three conditions: patient incapable and no surrogate available, danger to life or health, and immediate treatment needed.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Emergency exception (PDF p. 44)
questions.quote: The patient must be incapable of giving consent and no lawful surrogate is available

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Treating a patient without consent outside an emergency can lead to a claim of:
questions.rationale: Failure to obtain consent in non-emergencies can result in a claim of battery (unconsented touching).
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Informed consent (PDF p. 43)
questions.quote: Failure to obtain consent in situations other than emergencies can result in a claim of battery.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Temporary restraint of a confused patient to prevent self-injury, with safeguards, is an example of:
questions.rationale: Weak paternalism overrides the wishes of an incompetent or doubtfully competent patient; strong paternalism overrides a competent person.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Paternalism (PDF p. 45)
questions.quote: Granted all the proper institutional safeguards, restraints may be justified by weak paternalism.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: Overriding a competent patient's decision 'for his own good' is:
questions.rationale: Strong paternalism usurps a competent person's right to decide and is generally rejected ethically.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Paternalism (PDF p. 45)
questions.quote: strong (algo called extendeq paternalism, which attempts to overrule or override the wishes ofa competent person

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: Which nursing action violates patient privacy?
questions.rationale: Leaving curtains or doors open during a procedure exposes the patient and invades privacy.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Privacy (PDF p. 49)
questions.quote: Leaving the curtains or room door open while a treatment or procedure is being performed.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Two nurses discuss a patient's diagnosis in the hospital elevator. This violates:
questions.rationale: Discussing patients in elevators, cafeterias or outside the unit violates confidentiality.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Confidentiality (PDF p. 49)
questions.quote: even discussing patients in the elevator, cafeteria or any area outside the nursing unit

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: How does privacy differ from confidentiality?
questions.rationale: Privacy is about the person being free from intrusion; confidentiality protects information in a trust relationship.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Privacy vs. confidentiality (PDF p. 50)
questions.quote: Privacy talks about a person, but confidentiality is about information.

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: A doctor explains a diagnosis using so much jargon the family cannot understand. This violates veracity by:
questions.rationale: Veracity is violated by omission, commission (lying), or cloaking the truth in jargon so it is not understood.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Violations of veracity (PDF p. 52)
questions.quote: cloak the truth in so much medical jargon that the patient or her family will be unable to understand

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A Filipino family asks the nurse not to tell their father he has cancer. Which cultural trait explains this?
questions.rationale: In Filipino culture, families are often told first and may request non-disclosure to protect the patient.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Cultural considerations on truth telling (PDF p. 53)
questions.quote: family members are often informed before the patient, on serious diagnosis

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: A nurse manager must assign too few nurses to too many patients fairly. This is a question of:
questions.rationale: Distributive justice concerns fair allocation of benefits, burdens and scarce resources.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Distributive justice (PDF p. 55)
questions.quote: Nurse managers have to effectively allocate too few nurses to too many patients.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Patients in a clinic are seen in order of arrival unless medically urgent. This applies:
questions.rationale: Procedural justice (due process) means everyone receives the same treatment when their turn comes.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Procedural justice (PDF p. 55)
questions.quote: Procedural justice can be defined as due process.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Raising side rails to prevent a fall is an example of:
questions.rationale: Beneficence is acting for the good of others, e.g., preventing falls, giving prompt pain relief.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Beneficence (PDF p. 56)
questions.quote: Lifting side rails on a patient's hospital bed to prevent falls.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: A pregnant woman with uterine cancer has a hysterectomy, and the fetus dies as a foreseen side effect. Which principle is applied?
questions.rationale: Double effect permits an act with a good aim when the bad effect is foreseen but not directly intended and is proportionate.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Principle of double effect (PDF p. 57)
questions.quote: allow the removal of a life-threatening cancerous uterus, even though this procedure will bring the death of a fetus

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Directly encouraging or praising another's wrongful act is:
questions.rationale: Formal cooperation directly chooses the evil end or means (encouragement, advice) and is morally illicit.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Formal cooperation (PDF p. 58)
questions.quote: Formal cooperation occurs when the evil end or evil means are directly chosen by means of encouragement, praise, advice

questions.subject: NP I
questions.topic: Care of the Community: Health System, PHC, Epidemiology & Disaster
questions.stem: A barangay solves its sanitation problem itself before asking the city for help. This applies:
questions.rationale: Subsidiarity assigns each task to the smallest group able to do it; higher levels step in only when needed.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 2 Subsidiarity (PDF p. 60)
questions.quote: Ever-v task of societv should be assigned to the smallest possible group that can perform iL
